title: 🎙️ Repair Culture & Practical Tech
description: Today is about things you can fix, keep running, and pass on — repair culture, right-to-repair wins and setbacks, gear that outlives its manufacturer's support window, and the maker ethos of building to last rather than building to replace. We're interested in tools, devices, and projects where longevity, repairability, and self-sufficiency intersect, especially in rural and off-grid contexts where you can't just run to a repair shop. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Repair Culture & Practical Tech' — the right to repair movement, gear that outlasts its manufacturer, DIY fixes, and tools built for longevity.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical conflict; natural disasters without an engineering or preparedness angle; wildlife and conservation; working-lands policy; Indigenous governance; science discoveries with no DIY or hardware relevance; financial market news.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Hands-on hardware journalism counts fully even without an explicit right-to-repair hook.
- 80-100: Directly about repairability — right-to-repair legislation wins and losses, iFixit-style teardowns scoring repairability, gear designed for user serviceability, products outliving manufacturer support and how owners keep them running, permacomputing, vintage hardware still in active use, open-source hardware, Rossmann-style repair advocacy, 3D-printed replacement parts, battery replacement guides, rural and off-grid repair self-sufficiency.
- 55-79: Hands-on maker and DIY content — builds, modifications, hardware hacks, workshop projects, practical electronics guides with real technical depth, 3D printing hardware and filament, off-grid and solar gear, home lab hardware, tools and workshop equipment, battery and power tech. Most genuine hands-on hardware journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Gadget and device reviews with some technical substance; consumer electronics touching software longevity or ecosystem lock-in; hardware whose selling point is open firmware or modular design.
- 10-29: Surface-level product announcements, gadget speculation, leaked specs, general tech news with no hardware or repair angle.

ANCHORS: 'Framework Laptop 16 teardown: a 9/10 repairability score' → 98. 'Oregon's right-to-repair law takes effect' → 92. 'Building a solar-powered Raspberry Pi weather station' → 68. 'Samsung teases thinner bezels on next Galaxy' → 15.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] The list of AI insiders sounding the alarm on their own companies keeps growing
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Last week, OpenAI safety leader David Robinson resigned from the company, becoming the latest to join what is, in his words, a “parade of former colleagues” who have left roles at AI companies amid concerns about the tech or its use. In a subsequent essay for The Atlantic, he said the “trial and error” approach favored by AI companies must end.

Robinson is far from alone. Here’s a list of other AI researchers and employees who’ve made public warnings about their former employers.

ED NEWTON-REX

In November 2023, Ed Newton-Rex left his role leading the audio team at Stability AI, the maker of text-to-image tool Stable Diffusion, over concerns about the way copyrighted material was being used to train the tech.

“My opinion here doesn’t align with the generative AI industry’s current way of doing things,” Newton-Rex told Fast Company following his resignation, adding that he thought the industry’s prevailing outlook, paired with rapidly advancing tech, would be “very, very bad for creators.” 

Since then, he’s founded Fairly Trained, a nonprofit that issues certifications for AI companies whose data use meets certain requirements.

THE GROUP LETTER

On June 4, 2024, 13 current and former employees of top AI companies published a letter titled “A Right to Warn about Advanced Artificial Intelligence.” In it, they asserted that the technology poses risks ranging from “the further entrenchment of existing inequalities, to manipulation and misinformation, to the loss of control of autonomous AI systems potentially resulting in human extinction,” and expressed concerns about a lack of oversight. 

Signatories included former Google DeepMind employee Ramana Kumar, former Anthropic and current Google DeepMind employee Neel Nanda, who leads the company’s mechanistic interpretability team; and 11 current and former OpenAI employees, including Jacob Hilton, who now works for the Alignment Research Center; Daniel Kokotajlo, who founded and leads the nonprofit research group AI Futures Project; William Saunders, Carroll Wainwright, and Daniel Ziegler, the latter of whom now works for Anthropic; and six people who remained anonymous.

Prominent computer scientists Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, and “Godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton also endorsed the letter.

JAN LEIKE

In May 2024, OpenAI Superalignment team lead Jan Leike announced his departure on X, stating that “safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.” Leike, who has also worked at Google’s DeepMind, now heads Anthropic’s alignment team.

“Now is a good time to build institutional mechanisms to pace the frontier of AI development,” he said on X in September. “The industry is locked into an all-out scaling race to build superintelligence as quickly as possible, and we may need to give everyone more time for safety and alignment mitigations.” 

Leike added, “I’m not the only one who believes this,” linking to a statement titled “Pacing the Frontier” signed by 1,386 employees of major AI companies.

SUCHIR BALAJI

After graduating from the University of California, Berkeley, Suchir Balaji was hired by OpenAI, where he spent about four years working on ChatGPT and other projects.

He left the company in August 2024, on the same day as cofounder John Schulman, who said the timing was coincidental. Balaji blew the whistle on what he said were copyright infringements by Open AI, and published an essay online explaining how he thought ChatGPT’s outputs violated Fair Use law. 

That November, he was named as a potential witness in The New York Times’s lawsuit against OpenAI alleging willful copyright infringement.

The 26-year-old was found dead in his San Francisco apartment eight days later. His death was ruled a suicide, though his parents and others raised questions about that determination, as reported by The Guardian.

MRINANK SHARMA 

In February, Mrinank Sharma announced his departure from Anthropic, where he led the Safeguards Research team. 

“I continuously find myself reckoning with our situation,” Sharma wrote in his resignation letter, which he shared on X. “The world is in peril,” he continued, not just from AI and bioweapons, but “a whole series of interconnected crises.”

ALEX TURNER

Alex Turner left his job as a Google DeepMind research scientist in June, after a failed campaign to stop the company from signing a contract that allows the U.S. Pentagon to use its AI “for any lawful government purpose,” which he and others worry may allow for mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. 

Last month, he testified for a U.S. Senate hearing on rogue AI. “Often we think about the movements of our overseas adversaries, but now we must consider how we may be building adversaries at home by training misaligned AI systems,” he said in his written statement.

JACOB COXON

Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from the latter last month. 

“Neither company is acting responsibly,” he said in a viral X post. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

He went on to assert that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

In an interview with PBS in September, Coxon said an AI race with China “could be very bad, and that we should be taking pretty rapid actions for international coordination,” but that he believes the company leaders echoing that desire “are privately quite skeptical” of being able to achieve that cooperation.

MIKITA BALESNI, TOMEK KORBAK, AND JASMINE WANG

Last week, three OpenAI safety and alignment researchers were fired for mishandling sensitive misinformation, which one of them, Tomek Korbak, said online was due to how he’d communicated information to METR, the AI research nonprofit investigating OpenAI’s recent Hugging Face hacking incident.

“AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” the researchers said in the letter they sent to company leadership, which they published online on October 8. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.”

OpenAI released a statement the following day saying the researchers were fired after an internal investigation “found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information,” adding, “We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out.”

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover a human brain gene that can jump through DNA
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Scientists have discovered a human gene with a remarkable double life: it appears to play an important role in brain cells while still retaining the ability to jump around the genome. Called BC200, the gene evolved millions of years ago from a mobile piece of DNA known as a transposon, but unlike most genes that arose this way, it never lost its mobility. Researchers even found BC200 embedded inside a human poxvirus, suggesting it may have jumped from infected skin cells into the virus.

items.title: [Fast Company] A new employee was reprimanded for drinking 1 cup of coffee a day. An expert says the drink isn’t the real problem
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A new employee says they were reprimanded for drinking too much coffee.

The user took to Reddit to detail the situation, which unfolded at a job they’d started only a month prior. Each morning, they used the coffee machine and company-provided K-Cups and creamers. However, one day, a floor manager called them in and told them it was not typical to drink coffee every single morning. 

“I don’t imagine my boss having anything to say that would make this situation better, and I think it would just be unnecessary trouble,” the user wrote. “I do not want to be seen as someone who picks problems with people for small things.” 

To mitigate the problem, the new employee said they will bring their own K-Cups and creamers into the office moving forward. They also plan to document future interactions with the manager. “I need this job more than anything right now so I’m willing to look the other way since I’m not in the position at the moment to make any demands,” they said. 

Office culture

Many of the user’s fellow Redditors immediately sided with them.

“Even when free, I’ve never once heard of a single person being told they’re drinking too much. Especially not at one per day; that seems bizarre,” wrote one user.

Another commented, “As an intern, I was drinking five cups a day, and nobody batted an eye. It got to the point where the office manager told me where to restock the coffee pods if I saw we were running low. This is a super weird thing for them to be concerned about.” 

Experts say the user’s now-lingering tension over coffee usage could potentially lead to a deeper issue around comfort and safety at the workplace.

According to data from a national study by the Harris Poll, 60% of American workers report currently having a toxic supervisor, with more than 60% admitting they actively avoid their boss at work. 

“This type of behavior dramatically reduces psychological safety at that workplace. As a result, that new employee is more likely to quit and more likely to engage in activity to damage the company’s reputation,” Russell Clayton, an associate professor of instruction in the School of Management at the University of South Florida, told Inc. 

According to the Harris Poll, 61% of workers plan to switch jobs because of their boss as soon as the market allows. A separate survey done by the MIT Sloan Management Review analyzed 34 million employee profiles and found that toxic culture was the strongest predictor of employee attrition and was 10.4 times more important than compensation in predicting turnover.  

Get 1 Smart Business Story delivered straight to your inbox when you subscribe to Inc.’s free daily newsletter.

—By Moses Jeanfrancois, News Writer

This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com. 

Inc. is the voice of the American entrepreneur. We inspire, inform, and document the most fascinating people in business: the risk-takers, the innovators, and the ultra-driven go-getters that represent the most dynamic force in the American economy.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Studies link supportive childhoods and father involvement to well-being
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A study led by the University of Nottingham found that adults in the United Kingdom, United States and Japan who recalled more supportive childhood experiences reported better health, greater happiness and life satisfaction and lower anxiety [scitechdaily.com#1]. More supportive childhood experiences were also associated with stronger social connections, a greater sense of neighborhood belonging and more trust in others. The study, published Sept. 30 in the Journal of Happiness Studies, surveyed adults ages 18 to 34 [scitechdaily.com#1]. The findings show associations, not proof that childhood experiences caused adult outcomes: participants recalled their upbringing and reported their current well-being [scitechdaily.com#1]. Separately, a review of fatherhood research described links between sustained positive father involvement and children’s cognitive, social and emotional outcomes, while noting that the findings were correlational [time.com#1].

items.title: [Fast Company] Panda Express’s founders built a $7 billion empire. Now they’re helping 55,000 employees become homeowners
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Panda Express built an empire out of a single family’s restaurant. Now its founders are focused on helping their employees build something of their own.

Privately held and employing around 55,000 people, the Chinese food chain generates roughly $7 billion in annual sales and has grown into America’s largest Asian restaurant brand, with more than 2,500 locations across 49 states and a presence in 12 countries.

Behind that growth are two cofounders whose own paths to the U.S. weren’t so different from the immigrant employees they’re now trying to help. Andrew Cherng was born in China and raised in Taiwan and Japan before immigrating to the U.S. in 1966. Peggy Cherng was born in Myanmar and grew up in Hong Kong.

The two met at the University of Missouri and went on to become co-CEOs together, opening their first Panda Express in Glendale, California, in 1983. The restaurant initially launched as a more relaxed, faster-paced version of Panda Inn—the full-service Chinese restaurant Andrew started with his father roughly a decade earlier.

Subscribe to Inc. This Morning, Inc.’s free daily newsletter, to get the top stories of the day in your inbox.

Andrew told Inc. that the company’s mission has always extended beyond building a successful restaurant chain.

“Building Panda Restaurant Group for the past 50 years has been our American dream come true, and we are deeply committed to helping our associates achieve their own,” he said. “Homeownership is a major milestone for many of our team members, so we proactively equip them with the tools to reach it.”

Yet, over the past decade, that American dream of homeownership has slipped out of reach for millions of middle-class families. According to Gallup, U.S. homeownership has averaged just 61% since 2012, down from 70% between 2001 and 2011.

The pipeline of new buyers has thinned out even further, with the National Association of Realtors finding that first-time buyers made up just 21% of all homebuyers this year, the lowest share since the group began tracking the data in 1981.

That gap is even wider for immigrants. Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies reported foreign-born households had an average homeownership rate of just 56% in 2021, well below the native-born rate. That figure also varies widely by country of origin, ranging from a high of 73% among Vietnamese households down to just 29% among households from the Dominican Republic.

Despite the many obstacles standing between first-time buyers and homeownership, Andrew wants his Panda Express employees to focus on what’s possible rather than what’s holding them back.

To that end, Panda Express employees can access financial wellness benefits through the company’s Total Rewards Package, including optional training on budgeting, saving for a down payment, and homebuying seminars led by Panda’s in-house real estate legal team, part of a broader support system that also covers healthcare and higher education.

“This whole-person approach ensures associates can build sustainable careers and long-term financial security,” Andrew said.

That effort appears to be paying off: 63% of Panda Express managers are homeowners, with a median age of 34, above the national homeownership rate of roughly 35% for U.S. adults younger than 35.

“When you align closely with team members to help them reach their individual goals, strong retention follows,” Peggy told Inc.

At a moment when companies are cutting benefits, Panda Express’s bet on homeownership stands out. It may become a harder one for competitors to ignore.

—By Amaya Nichole, News Writer
